description:
We are an international team all living full-time in Brazil.

We are passionate about finding creative solutions to problems, as well as for learning about different cultures and the ways people enjoy the world. (And hopefully space)
summary:
Debris is a mobile web game that turns picking up litter into a journey through the history of space. Children photograph and dispose of a piece of litter they find in their local neighbourhood; unlocking the next chapter of a story about 13 machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Each chapter explains what the machine was, why it was sent, what it discovered and how it still helps us, with real NASA photos and sources. 

Debris makes the history of forgotten hardware personal and links it to a real action they take to help clean up Earth, as well as earning a patch for the child's digital explorer jacket. A shared “Litter to the Moon” tower and counter shows everyone in the world's combined impact by picking up trash in their local communities.

It is built for children: no accounts, no location tracking, photos are never stored and dangerous items are flagged for an adult. It works in English, Spanish and Portuguese and users can pick a second storyteller inspired by Florianópolis’s Boi de Mamão local folklore tradition. The aim being to expand the selection of custom storytellers based upon local stories familiar to children in different communities around the world.
details:
We uploaded a 3 minute animated explainer to Youtube (linked in resources section below) that helps explain our project. Below we have further detail for you:

What does Debris do?
Debris is a mobile web game for children aged 7 to 12 (but open to all ages above) that turns picking up litter into a journey through space history.
A child photographs a piece of litter and AI checks it. They put it in the trash and that unlocks the next chapter of a story about 13 machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, from Surveyor 3 in 1967 to the Ingenuity helicopter.

Each chapter explains what the machine was, why it was sent, what it discovered and how it still helps us today, with real NASA photos and sources.

Each chapter also earns a patch for the child’s 3D explorer jacket.
The ‘impact’ tab provides a “Litter to the Moon” tower showing how much litter everyone using the app has picked up together, compared with landmarks on the way to the Moon, as well as showing the number of pieces of trash collected by the users of the app.

What benefits does Debris have?
The main benefits are:

  • Children associate learning about real space history and science with being rewarded.
  • Children learn not only what we know about space, but how we know about it and the tools used to obtain the knowledge we have.
  • Children are taught and encourage to clean up litter in their local communities. Earning both rewards on their 3D Jacket, unlocking stories and also seeing in the ‘impact’ tab, just how much trash they have been able to collect alongside everyone else in the world to make a difference to our planet.
  • Parents and teachers can trust it: no location tracking, photos are never stored, and dangerous items are flagged for an adult.
  • It’s free, needs no install or account, and works in any phone browser in English, Spanish and Portuguese. There is even a localised narrator for children in Florianopolis where we live, which creates a ‘Boi de Mamão’ narrator and twist to the chapters about space history - making learning about space more familiar to their local stories they know and love.

What is the intended impact of Debris?
We want to create a win:win:win, where children are encouraged to help clean their local communities and environments and in doing so taught that learning can be a reward. We wanted to:

  1. Create a generation of children that grow up to desire keeping our planet clean and healthy.
  2. Create a generation of children that genuinely believe learning is a reward.
  3. Teach children not only about what we know about space, but how we learnt what we know and how we have shaped our technology and space practices.

We expect that not only will adults with their children use the app on a one by one basis, but also local communities and schools. We already spoke with adults working with children who were genuinely interested in trying out and using the app.

The aim is to make the children and adults who use the app not only have a fun time cleaning up their neighbourhood and learning about space history, but also to help them feel that what they do really makes a difference; with the ‘impact’ tab showing that they are part of a huge community of people picking up trash and helping clean our planet.

What tools, coding languages, hardware and software did we use?
Languages: JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with Node.js on the server. Story content is in JSON; illustrations are SVG.

Libraries and APIs: three.js for the 3D jacket, the Web Audio API for sound, the browser’s speech feature for read-aloud, and the Anthropic SDK.

AI: Claude (Anthropic) checks each photo for litter, its type, the right bin and anything dangerous. We also used Claude as an assistant for research, fact-checking, writing and producing the promo video. Additionally we used Grok Bot and Perplexity to help.

Design: Blender for the 3D jacket model.

Hosting and code: GitHub, with Netlify or Railway for hosting.

Hardware: smartphones for testing and filming, and windows and mac laptops for development.

Data: NASA mission pages (NSSDCA and NASA Science) and NASA images.

How is our project creative?
We have created a free, easy to access web app which can be used by adult supervisors and children on a one to one basis or in school or community groups.


Debris links two kinds of things we leave behind: the machines left on other worlds and the litter left on our own. Instead of reading about forgotten spacecraft, children “wake them up” by cleaning up their own neighbourhood. Each machine becomes a patch on a jacket they can spin, and the world’s litter becomes a tower growing toward the Moon.

We also added a second storyteller inspired by Florianópolis’s boi de mamão folk tradition. In the play, the bull falls silent and everyone brings him back to life, just as children bring forgotten explorers back to life. Bernúncia, the ‘dragon’ of the play, gobbles up each piece of litter. Adding in this bonus narrator in the profile section that users can choose enables the children to get a ‘local, fun touch’ added to the chapters and helps them learn with characters they are familiar from their local communities and traditions.

The aim is to expand and create more localised narrators (which come with little fun localised amendments and cameos to the chapters) for each community which embraces the app and wants to use it to teach their children to help clean our planet and learn about the how and why of space exploration.

We felt that using AI to detect trash and encourage children to clean up their own planet, to then be rewarded by learning about how we have explored space and other planets and space objects was a fun idea and one that only brings benefits.

What factors did we consider?

Who it’s for: children aged 7 to 12. We kept the language short and simple, added a “Listen” button that reads every chapter aloud, and used kid-friendly comparisons to explain numbers.

Accuracy: every fact was checked against NASA mission pages, and each chapter links its sources. Where we couldn’t confirm a detail, we removed it.

Safety: children are reminded to wear gloves and bring an adult. If the scanner sees something dangerous, such as glass or needles, it tells the child to stop and ask an adult, and it never awards a patch for it, so there’s no reason to touch it.

Privacy: no accounts, no names, no location. Photos are checked once by AI and never stored. Photos with humans in them are not permitted.

Honest impact: the shared counter only goes up when a child confirms a piece is in the bin, and each piece counts once.

Accessibility and reach: it runs in any phone browser with no install, works in English, Spanish and Portuguese, supports screen readers and reduced motion, and fits small screens.

Culture: the boi de mamão storyteller lets local children see their own traditions in the story, and it credits the tradition it comes from.
